You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
" *

Adds all the elements of the given arrays into a new array.

*

The new array contains all of the element of array1 followed * by all of the elements array2. When an array is returned, it is always * a new array.

* * 
     * ArrayUtils.addAll(null, null)     = null
     * ArrayUtils.addAll(array1, null)   = cloned copy of array1
     * ArrayUtils.addAll(null, array2)   = cloned copy of array2
     * ArrayUtils.addAll([], [])         = []
     * ArrayUtils.addAll([null], [null]) = [null, null]
     * ArrayUtils.addAll(["a", "b", "c"], ["1", "2", "3"]) = ["a", "b", "c", "1", "2", "3"]
     *
* * @param array1 the first array whose elements are added to the new array, may be null * @param array2 the second array whose elements are added to the new array, may be null * @return The new array, null if both arrays are null. * The type of the new array is the type of the first array, * unless the first array is null, in which case the type is the same as the second array. * @since 2.1 "

Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- What the test does:
  - Valid case: Number[] n = ArrayUtils.addAll(new Number[]{1}, new Long[]{2L}); This should succeed because a Long is a Number, and the destination array is of component type Number.
  - Invalid case: n = ArrayUtils.addAll(new Integer[]{1}, new Long[]{2L}); This should fail clearly, and the test expects an IllegalArgumentException.

- Relevant implementation:
  - org.apache.commons.lang3.ArrayUtils.addAll(T[], T...) at lines 2952–2965:
    - Determines the destination component type from array1: final Class<?> type1 = array1.getClass().getComponentType();
    - Allocates joinedArray of that type: (T[]) Array.newInstance(type1, ...);
    - Copies array1, then blindly copies array2: System.arraycopy(array2, 0, joinedArray, array1.length, array2.length); (line 2962)
    - There’s a comment “// Check if problem is incompatible types” but no check is actually implemented.

- How the failure occurs:
  - In the invalid case, array1 is Integer[] so joinedArray is Integer[].
  - array2 is Long[]. System.arraycopy tries to store Long elements into an Integer[] destination.
  - This violates array store compatibility and the JVM throws ArrayStoreException at the arraycopy call (line 2962), matching the bug report’s stack trace.
  - The test only catches IllegalArgumentException, so the uncaught ArrayStoreException causes the test to fail.

- Root cause:
  - The method does not validate type compatibility between the component types (or elements) of array2 and the destination array type derived from array1 before performing System.arraycopy.
  - As a result, incompatible mixes result in ArrayStoreException instead of the intended/clear IllegalArgumentException. The existing comment hints at the intended check, but it’s missing.

- Consequences:
  - Valid mixed-type merge works when array1’s component type is a common supertype (e.g., Number[] with Long[]).
  - Invalid mixes (e.g., Integer[] with Long[]) bubble up as ArrayStoreException, contradicting the test’s expectation and the aim for clearer error reporting.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
